common_name: Telfair Citrangequat (Historic Swingle-Bred Cold-Hardy Kumquat Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Telfair is one of the lesser-known historic citrangequats bred alongside Thomasville and Sinton for extreme cold hardiness.

directions: Telfair citrangequat was bred by USDA scientist Walter Swingle in the early 1900s alongside the better-known Thomasville and Sinton citrangequats, crossing a Willits citrange (trifoliate orange x sweet orange) with Nagami kumquat to push edible citrus culture into colder climates. The small, rounded, thin-skinned orange fruit is tart with a mild kumquat sweetness in the peel, best suited to marmalade, candied peel, or ade rather than fresh eating out of hand. Mature wood tolerates temperatures down into the single digits Fahrenheit, similar to its Thomasville sibling, making it a hardy novelty planting for Gulf Coast gardeners who want citrus outside the usual protected range. Give young trees a sheltered, sunny site with excellent drainage and winter protection for their first two or three seasons.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Citrus Germplasm and Swingle Citrangequat Breeding
University of Georgia Extension — Cold-Hardy Citrus for the Southeast
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Cold-Hardy Citrus Hybrids

common_name: Bouquet de Fleurs Sour Orange (Fragrant Dwarf Ornamental Orange)

planting.note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Bouquet de Fleurs is a naturally dwarf, heavy-blooming sour orange selection well suited to containers as well as open-ground Gulf Coast plantings.

directions: Bouquet de Fleurs is an old Florida sour orange selection grown chiefly for its exceptionally heavy, powerfully fragrant flush of white spring blossoms, historically harvested for neroli-scented orange flower water and perfumery. The naturally compact, low, spreading tree tops out around 6 to 8 feet, fitting large containers or small dooryard plantings better than standard sour orange seedlings. Like other sour oranges, it carries the same cold hardiness that made Citrus aurantium the traditional rootstock and hedge citrus of the Gulf South, shrugging off brief dips into the low-to-mid 20s Fahrenheit once established. The tart, seedy, puckering fruit hangs on the tree for months and makes excellent marmalade or liqueur flavoring, though it is not meant for fresh eating.
sources: University of California Riverside Givaudan Citrus Variety Collection
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Sour Orange and Cold-Hardy Citrus

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after frost danger passes, in full sun and well-drained soil; Keraji is a cold-hardy Japanese mandarin known for its distinctive tart, lemonade-like flavor rather than typical sweet mandarin taste.

directions: Keraji is a small, cold-hardy mandarin developed in Japan and long grown on Kikai-jima island in the Ryukyus, prized among cold-hardy citrus hobbyists for a tart, distinctly lemonade-like flavor unlike typical sweet mandarins. The thornless, vigorous tree can reach 15 feet or more where winters stay mild, but responds well to pruning for a more compact dooryard or large-container size. Mature wood has been reported to tolerate brief drops to around 12°F, making it noticeably hardier than standard mandarins and a good candidate for pushing citrus culture into cooler pockets of zone 8b Gulf Coast gardens. The small, seedy, yellow-orange fruit ripens in winter and is used more often for juice and ade than fresh peeling and eating.
sources: University of California Riverside Givaudan Citrus Variety Collection
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Cold-Hardy Citrus Selections

planting.note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Nansho Daidai is among the most cold-hardy evergreen citrus known, with documented Deep South specimens surviving winter lows near 0°F.

directions: Nansho Daidai, botanically Citrus taiwanica, is a vigorous, thorny sour orange type that the Japanese named and popularized during their administration of Taiwan, valued today by cold-hardy citrus growers for its exceptional toughness. Documented specimens in the Deep South have come through winter lows near 0°F with little to no leaf drop, placing it among the hardiest evergreen citrus grown in the United States, on par with Thomasville citrangequat and trifoliate orange hybrids. The orange-sized, acid-bitter fruit is not eaten fresh but substitutes well for lemon or sour orange juice in ades, marinades, and sauces, and the tree is also used as an understock for other citrus. Plant in full sun with excellent drainage and expect a large, vigorous, well-armed tree that needs little winter protection once established in zone 8 Gulf Coast gardens.
sources: University of California Riverside Givaudan Citrus Variety Collection
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Cold-Hardy Citrus for Texas

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring after frost danger passes, in well-drained soil in full sun; Sampson was the very first tangelo produced, an 1897 cross of Dancy tangerine and Bowen grapefruit, and remains grown chiefly as a heirloom curiosity.

directions: Sampson was the first tangelo ever produced, bred by Walter Swingle in 1897 at Eustis, Florida by crossing Dancy tangerine with pollen from Bowen grapefruit, decades before the more familiar Orlando and Minneola tangelos followed from similar parentage. The medium, globose, thin-skinned fruit is juicy and tangy with a distinctive bittersweet tang and a heavy seed count, prized more by citrus historians and collectors than commercial growers, though it remains an interesting dooryard curiosity and occasional rootstock. Cold hardiness falls between its tangerine and grapefruit parents, tolerating brief dips into the upper 20s Fahrenheit but needing more winter protection than satsuma or true mandarins in zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens. Grow it in full sun on well-drained soil as a conversation-piece heirloom alongside more productive modern citrus.
sources: USDA National Agricultural Library — Swingle Citrus Breeding Collection
University of California Riverside Givaudan Citrus Variety Collection
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Heirloom Citrus Varieties

common_name: Willits Citrange (Historic Cold-Hardy Swingle Orange-Trifoliate Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Willits was one of Walter Swingle's original 1897 citrange hybrids and later became a parent of the Telfair and Thomasville citrangequats.

directions: Willits was among the first citrange hybrids Walter Swingle produced in his original 1897 trifoliate orange x sweet orange crosses, made in response to the catastrophic Florida freezes of the 1890s that wiped out groves as far south as Orlando. It later proved important as a parent of the Telfair and Thomasville citrangequats, lending its cold hardiness to those kumquat hybrids as breeders continued pushing citrus culture northward. The tart, seedy, orange-like fruit carries more acid than a true sweet orange and suits marmalade or ade far better than fresh eating, but the tree's trifoliate-influenced hardiness lets it survive freezes near 0°F that would kill standard oranges outright. Site it in full sun with sharp drainage and expect a semi-deciduous, lightly thorny habit typical of citrange hybrids, especially in colder Gulf Coast winters.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Citrus Germplasm and Swingle Citrange Breeding
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Cold-Hardy Citrus Rootstocks and Hybrids
Purdue University Center for New Crops — Sundry Citrus Hybrids and Rootstocks
